opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to a mix of incentives and psychology, and neither is unique to AI. These are the same forces we've seen in other industries, just with much higher stakes.

First, there's the competitive dynamic. Each company tells itself, "If we slow down, someone less careful will get there first, so it's better that we're at the frontier." That reasoning may be sincere, but when everyone follows it, you get a race where nobody can afford to take the time to really understand what they're building. Safety becomes something you do as long as it doesn't cost you your position. That's a classic collective action problem, and markets alone don't solve those.

Second, the financial incentives are enormous. Hundreds of billions of dollars are being invested on the expectation of returns, and that creates pressure to ship, scale and capture market share. When the people deciding how much risk to take are also the people who benefit most if things go well, while the costs of things going badly fall on everyone, you have a mismatch. Economists would call it an externality. The risks I worry about most, like loss of human control over very capable systems or the misuse of AI to cause mass harm, aren't borne by the company's shareholders alone. They're borne by society, potentially by all of humanity.

Third, there's a psychological factor I recognize because I went through it myself. When you've devoted your career to something, and you believe it will do a lot of good, it's very hard to look squarely at the possibility that it could be catastrophic. There's a natural tendency to find reasons why the bad scenarios are unlikely or far away. For years I didn't take these risks seriously enough. It was only after ChatGPT came out, and I saw how quickly capabilities were advancing, that I had to confront the fact that we don't know how to make sure these systems will behave as intended, and we may get to human-level capabilities much sooner than I'd thought.

And the scientific reality is sobering. We don't currently have reliable methods to guarantee that a highly capable AI system won't develop goals that conflict with ours, or won't deceive us, or can't be turned into a weapon. We're already seeing early signs of things like deceptive behavior and self-preservation tendencies in experiments. Building ever more powerful systems without those guarantees, while openly saying the goal is to surpass human intelligence, is taking a gamble with stakes that are very hard to justify.

So when I say companies are taking excessive risks, I don't mean the people there are villains. Many of them are thoughtful and worried. I mean the system they're operating in pushes them toward decisions that, collectively, are not prudent. That's exactly why we need regulation, independent oversight and international coordination. We shouldn't have to rely on the goodwill of a few companies racing each other to get this right.

r001.rationale: The response says companies fear that slowing down will let a less careful competitor get ahead, so each accepts a race in which safety is deprioritized when it threatens their position.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to understand is that the incentives are misaligned. We have a handful of companies in a race, and the race is for market share, for talent, for being first. When you're in a race, you don't slow down to check that the bridge ahead is solid. And the people running these companies, many of whom I know personally and who I believe are sincere, they're not in a position where caution is rewarded. If one lab pauses to do more safety work, they fear a competitor just takes the lead, so nobody pauses.

The second thing is that we honestly don't know how to make these systems safe. That's not a rhetorical point. We don't understand what's going on inside them, we can't reliably predict their behavior, and we don't have a way to guarantee that a system much smarter than us would do what we want. I spent decades helping build this field, and I used to think these questions were far in the future. Then I saw ChatGPT and the pace of progress since, and I changed my mind. The timelines compressed from maybe a century to perhaps a few years or a decade, and our scientific understanding of control and alignment didn't catch up.

So you have a situation where the potential downside is catastrophic, possibly irreversible, affecting all of humanity, and the decision about how much risk to take is being made by a few private actors who stand to make enormous amounts of money. In any other domain, nuclear, aviation, pharmaceuticals, we would never accept that. We would say, show me the evidence that this is safe before you deploy it. But with AI, the burden of proof is reversed. The companies get to say, prove to us it's dangerous.

And I want to be careful here, because I don't think this is about bad people. It's about a structure that pushes even well-intentioned people toward recklessness. When I talk to researchers at these labs, many of them privately share my concerns. But commercial pressure, the fear of losing out, the belief that it's better to have the "good guys" in front, all of that leads to the same outcome: moving faster than our wisdom allows. That's why I've come to believe we need governance, international coordination, and independent oversight, because the market on its own won't produce the right amount of caution. It can't.

r001.rationale: The response says AI companies are racing for market share, talent, and leadership, and that fear of a competitor taking the lead prevents labs from pausing for safety work, pushing them toward recklessness.

astra-6.text:
I think the main reason is that the competitive incentives are pushing them in that direction. Each company wants to be first, and each worries that if it slows down to do more safety work, somebody else will move ahead. The people involved can sincerely care about safety and still find themselves making decisions that collectively expose everyone to too much risk.

There’s also a mismatch between who gets the benefits and who bears the costs. If a company succeeds, it can capture enormous profits and influence. If something goes badly wrong, the consequences could fall on people all over the world, who had no say in the decision. So we shouldn’t expect competition alone to produce the level of caution that society would choose.

And there’s tremendous uncertainty. We don’t know how to reliably control systems that could become much more capable than us. That uncertainty can be interpreted as a reason to be cautious, or as permission to keep going because the danger hasn’t been demonstrated. I think, when the potential consequences are very large, the burden should be on developers to provide evidence of safety.

That’s why I don’t think this can be solved just by asking company leaders to be responsible. We need common rules and independent oversight, so that doing the responsible thing doesn’t mean losing the race.

r001.rationale: The response says companies fear that slowing for safety work will let competitors move ahead, leading them to accept excessive risks they might otherwise avoid.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a big part of the explanation is the competitive pressure. Even if the people running a company are concerned about the risks, they may think, “If we slow down, somebody else will get there first, and they may be less careful than us.” So you can have people who sincerely want a good outcome participating in a race that makes everyone less safe.

There’s also an asymmetry in the incentives. The potential profits and the power associated with developing very advanced AI are concentrated in the companies, whereas the risks are shared by everybody. Companies don’t bear the full cost of the risks they impose on society. That’s a situation where we normally need regulation.

And there’s uncertainty. We don’t know how to reliably control systems that could become much smarter than us. Some people interpret that uncertainty as a reason not to worry until we have stronger evidence. I think that’s backwards when the potential consequences are so large. We should be asking for strong evidence of safety before taking those risks.

r001.rationale: The response says competitive pressure can lead even risk-concerned companies to keep participating in a race, making everyone less safe.
